teaser: A bouquet that could never have existed, caught in a second that never happened.
review_notes:
Year: the Rijksmuseum dates this work broadly (c. 1650-1683); 1665 is the catalog date.
Symbolic readings (butterfly as soul or resurrection, snail and caterpillar as earthbound life, wheat as bread of the Eucharist, window reflection as a cross) are common scholarly interpretations, presented as such.
Tulip prices: 'more than a house on an Amsterdam canal' is the frequently repeated peak figure from the 1637 mania: check wording.
Tulip breaking virus identified in the 1920s, spread by aphids.
De Heem's biography: born Utrecht 1606, moved to Antwerp in the mid 1630s, back in Utrecht c. 1667-1672, returned to Antwerp, died 1683 or 1684.
Flower identifications (viburnum 'snowball', fritillary, honeysuckle, morning glory, poppy anemone) are by eye from the image.
Support and size: believed to be oil on copper, about 54.5 x 36.5 cm (matches the image proportions): check against the Rijksmuseum record.
The 'fellow painter' is Joachim von Sandrart, paraphrased, not quoted.

lesson.text: A butterfly has just closed its wings on a poppy. A caterpillar is halfway along a stem. A snail has reached the corner of the stone ledge and stretched out its horns. Hold your breath: in one more second all three will have moved.
That second is what Jan Davidsz. de Heem pretends to have caught. The feeling is strong enough that it takes a while to notice the trick. This instant never happened. It could not have.
Start with the smallest traveler. A caterpillar is crossing the bouquet near the top. Where?

spots.title: Mid-crawl
spots.text: An orange and black caterpillar arches its back on the stalk just under the great red poppy. De Heem paints it in the middle of a step, which is why the whole picture seems to be happening right now.

lesson.text: Here is the trick. Tulips and narcissi bloom in early spring. Roses and poppies come in summer. Wheat ripens at the end of it, and morning glories open in the warm months too. In the 1600s there were no heated flower farms and no air freight. No vase in Europe ever held these stems together.
The bouquet is a montage. De Heem assembled it in the studio from separate studies, so the “frozen instant” is really many months of looking, folded into one picture.

Why go to the trouble? Partly because buyers wanted the best of every season, permanently. A real bouquet wilts within a week. A painted one keeps a tulip open for centuries. And some of these flowers were treasures in their own right.

lesson.title: The expensive ones
lesson.text: At the top right, two tulips lean out of the bouquet.

spots.title: The flamed tulip
spots.text: Red streaks on white, like brushed flames. Tulips with this pattern were the most wanted flowers in Holland. De Heem turns it to face you, like a portrait.

spots.title: Its dark twin
spots.text: A second tulip, deep purple and white, opens wide just behind. Its petals have started to curl outward: this bloom is already past its best.

spots.title: A checkered bell
spots.text: Lower down hangs a fritillary, a nodding spring flower with a checkerboard pattern on its petals. Collectors prized such oddities of nature.

lesson.text: During the tulip craze that peaked in early 1637, a single bulb of a rare flamed variety could change hands for more than the price of a house on an Amsterdam canal. A painting of one, even by a famous master, was the bargain.

Nobody then knew what made a tulip “break” into flames. The cause was found only in the 1920s: a virus, carried from plant to plant by aphids. The most admired flowers in the Dutch Republic were, in fact, sick.
So there is illness inside the beauty, and De Heem seems to enjoy that thought. The longer you stay, the more the bouquet turns out to be inhabited. Something is eating it.

lesson.title: The small appetites
lesson.text: Three places where the perfect bouquet is under attack.

spots.title: Ants on the roses
spots.text: Tiny black ants walk over the white rose and across the pale pink bloom below it. They are drawn by the sweetness, like everyone else.

spots.title: A spoiled leaf
spots.text: At the far left a leaf has turned orange and brown, spotted with decay. De Heem could have left it out. He put it where the eye wanders after the big blooms.

spots.title: The snail
spots.text: A yellow snail with a dark spiral band slides across the corner of the ledge, horns out, heading for the fallen stems.

lesson.text: For a 17th-century viewer this was more than natural history. Flowers that fade stood for human life: lovely and short. The creatures could carry meaning too. A butterfly, which comes out of a dead-looking cocoon, was a common image of the soul or of resurrection. Caterpillars and snails stayed down on the earth.

One more element points the same way. Ears of wheat hang among the stems and lie on the ledge. Wheat makes bread, and bread, for a Christian viewer, meant the Eucharist and the promise of life after death. In Catholic Antwerp, where De Heem spent much of his career, such hints were common.
The painter left a trace of the room he worked in. It is somewhere on the glass vase. Can you see it?

spots.title: The window
spots.text: On the curve of the vase, a bright patch crossed by dark bars: the reflection of a studio window. It tells you where the light comes from, the upper left, and some viewers read its bars as a cross.

lesson.text: That reflection is the only sign of a world outside. Everything else sits against near-black, a device De Heem used so that each color would burn at full strength. He lays the paint on in thin, clear layers called glazes, one over another, which is why the reds seem lit from inside. The support helps: this picture is painted on a sheet of copper, far smoother than canvas.

De Heem was born in Utrecht in 1606 and moved to Antwerp in his thirties. A fellow painter later explained why: in Antwerp you could get rare fruit of every kind, large plums, peaches, grapes and more, in better condition to paint from life.

The move changed him. In the Dutch north, still lifes were sober and exact. In Flemish Antwerp they were lavish, tumbling, full of color. De Heem joined the two, northern precision with southern abundance, and nearly every flower painter of the next century learned from him.

spots.title: The butterfly
spots.text: A red admiral, wings half closed, shows its dark mottled underside and a flash of red. It sits at the very top of the picture, above everything that crawls.

spots.title: The great poppy
spots.text: A shaggy, scarlet double poppy, the largest bloom in the bouquet. Poppies were linked with sleep, and through sleep, with death.

spots.title: Pea pods
spots.text: Two fat green pods dangle from a curling tendril. A vegetable has climbed into the bouquet: this is a garden, not a florist's arrangement.

spots.title: Snowball
spots.text: A cluster of small white blossoms, with an orange insect resting on it. The white is built from soft grays and only a few bright touches.

spots.title: Morning glory
spots.text: Blue trumpet flowers with a white star inside. A morning glory opens at dawn and closes within the day, a short life even by a flower's standards.

spots.title: Fallen wheat
spots.text: A golden ear of wheat lies on the stone ledge, each grain and bristle painted separately.

spots.title: The red flower on the ledge
spots.text: A red bloom has dropped onto the stone and faces us. With its partner on the right, it frames the dark foot of the vase.

spots.title: Honeysuckle
spots.text: Red and cream tubes fan out like fingers. De Heem lets it stray from the bunch so its silhouette reads clearly against the dark.

lesson.text: Go back to the butterfly, the caterpillar and the snail. They made the picture feel like one caught second. Now you know it is closer to the opposite: spring, summer and harvest, bloom and rot, all held on a copper plate about 54 cm (21 inches) tall. The instant is the one thing here that was invented.

quiz.question: Why could this bouquet never have stood in a real vase in the 1600s?
options: The flowers bloom in different seasons
quiz.explanation: Spring tulips, summer roses and ripe wheat could not be gathered at the same time.

quiz.question: What causes the flamed pattern on the tulips?
quiz.explanation: The cause was identified in the 1920s as a virus carried by aphids.

quiz.question: What can you see reflected on the glass vase?
quiz.explanation: A bright patch with dark bars shows the window that lit the studio.

quiz.question: What did a butterfly commonly stand for in such paintings?
quiz.explanation: Because it emerges from a cocoon, it was an image of the soul and of new life.

quiz.question: Why did De Heem move to Antwerp, according to a fellow painter?
options: To paint from rarer and finer fruit
quiz.explanation: Antwerp offered rare fruit in better condition to paint from life.

quiz.question: What is this picture painted on?
quiz.explanation: The smooth copper plate helps the thin layers of color glow.

facts.text: At the height of the tulip craze, a rare bulb could cost more than a canal house.
facts.explanation: Prices for flamed tulips peaked in early 1637 at astonishing levels.

facts.text: De Heem painted the whole bouquet in one sitting from a real arrangement.
facts.explanation: He combined separate studies of flowers that bloom months apart.

facts.text: Every leaf and petal in the picture is shown in perfect condition.
facts.explanation: Ants crawl on the roses and one leaf is spotted with decay.
